title: NAFNet — the paper that asked whether any of this is necessary
lead: Chen, Chu, Zhang and Sun, ECCV 2022 (MEGVII). While everyone else added mechanisms, this paper removed them, and reached a higher number. Its two derivations are the most elegant reasoning in the modern half of this deck.

eqs.tex: GLU( X, f, g, σ )  =  f(X) ⊙ σ( g(X) )                    GELU( x )  =  x · Φ(x)
eqs.where: the gated linear unit, and GELU — Φ is the standard normal CDF

eqs.tex: ⟹   GELU is a special case of GLU   with f, g = identity and σ = Φ
eqs.where: which suggests GLU is a *generalisation of activation functions* — and that it might replace them
eqs.latex: \Longrightarrow\quad \mathrm{GELU}\ \text{is a special case of GLU, with}\ f, g = \mathrm{id}\ \text{and}\ \sigma = \Phi

eqs.tex: SimpleGate( X, Y )  =  X ⊙ Y
eqs.where: split the feature map in half along the channel axis and multiply the halves. That is the entire activation function.

bullets: **The key observation.** GLU *itself contains nonlinearity and does not depend on σ* — f(X) ⊙ g(X) is nonlinear because a product of two linear maps is not linear. So the gate alone supplies it.
**Compare implementations.** GELU needs 0.5x(1 + tanh[√(2/π)(x + 0.044715x³)]). SimpleGate is one element-wise multiplication — *That's all*.
**Applied again to channel attention**, CA(X) = X ∗ Ψ(X) reduces to **SCA(X) = X ∗ W pool(X)**: one pooling, one 1×1, no Sigmoid, no ReLU.
**The result.** No activation functions anywhere — *the first work demonstrating that the nonlinear activation functions may not be necessary for SOTA computer vision methods.*

notes: Deliver the GELU-as-GLU step slowly. It is a genuinely surprising piece of reasoning and it is the thing a TA is most likely to ask you to reproduce on a whiteboard.

title: The ablation ladder — every rung is a controlled experiment
lead: Starting from PlainNet — convolution, ReLU, shortcut, in a single-stage U-Net — each row changes exactly one thing. All at a ≈16 GMAC budget, 256×256 patches, batch 32, 200 K iterations, Adam, PSNR loss.
foot: **Three readings.** (a) The largest single gain is **LayerNorm**, worth +0.44 dB on denoising and +3.39 dB on deblurring — not because normalisation is magic but because it *stabilises training at a ten-times larger learning rate*. The architecture did not improve; the optimisation did. (b) Both simplifications **improved** results — SimpleGate beats GELU, SCA beats CA. (c) The headline: **40.30 dB on SIDD, exceeding the previous state of the art by 0.28 dB with less than half its computational cost**, and 36.69 dB on GoPro, exceeding the previous best by 0.38 dB with **8.4%** of its cost.
cite: NAFNet22 §3.3–3.6, §4, abstract — values as printed
notes: The LayerNorm row is the honest lesson of the whole architecture branch and worth saying out loud: a large share of reported architectural progress in restoration is optimisation progress wearing a costume.

title: SCUNet — fix the training data, not only the network
lead: Zhang, Li, Liang, Cao, Zhang, Tang, Fan, Timofte and Van Gool, *Machine Intelligence Research* 20(6), 2023 (ETH Zürich). Same first author as DnCNN, six years later, attacking the assumption DnCNN made rather than the architecture DnCNN built.

bullets: The motivation is complementarity: *different methods for image denoising have complementary image prior modeling ability and can be incorporated to boost the performance*.

**The block.** A 1×1 convolution, then split the feature map in two. One half goes to a **Swin Transformer block** (non-local), the other to a **residual convolutional block** (local). Concatenate, 1×1, residual connection.
Plug it into a standard UNet backbone. Local and non-local priors run **in parallel** rather than one replacing the other.
**9.663 M parameters** — a third of Restormer's, a twelfth of NAFNet's. ^2^

**The premise, bluntly:** a model trained by AWGN *performs poorly for most of real images due to noise assumption mismatch*. Nevertheless AWGN removal *is fair to test the effectiveness of different network architecture designs*.

**So synthesise realistic noise.** The pipeline samples Gaussian (3-D generalised, with a 3×3 covariance matrix for R/G/B correlation), **Poisson**, **speckle**, **JPEG**, and **camera sensor noise**.
**Sensor noise goes through a real ISP** — invert a clean image to raw, add read and shot noise there, then run demosaicing, white balance, tone mapping and gamma forward.
**Plus resizing, random shuffling and double degradation**, because *upscaling would lead AWGN to be spatially correlated* and real images may be resized or JPEG compressed repeatedly.

foot: **The lesson worth stating.** Every other paper in Part V competes on the architecture. SCUNet's four contributions include *a hand-designed noise synthesis model, which can be used to train a general-purpose blind image denoising model*. The distribution you train on is a design surface, and it is the one that most directly attacks the AWGN assumption named on slide 7.
cite: SCUNet23 abstract, §1, §3.1, §3.2, Fig. 1 · parameter count [measured], commit 52e440a
notes: SCUNet is the bridge between Part V and Part VII. It is the paper that says the benchmark itself is the problem, which is the argument slide 82 then proves with the SIDD numbers.

title: State-space models — a third answer to bottleneck 3
lead: Guo, Li, Dai, Ouyang, Ren and Xia, ECCV 2024 (Tsinghua Shenzhen / Shenzhen University / ByteDance). If attention is quadratic and windowed attention surrenders globality, borrow a mechanism from control theory that is global *and* linear.

eqs.tex: h′(t)  =  A h(t)  +  B x(t) ,          y(t)  =  C h(t)  +  D x(t)
eqs.where: a continuous linear time-invariant system — the S4 formulation. N is the state size; A ∈ R^{N×N}, B ∈ R^{N×1}, C ∈ R^{1×N}, D ∈ R

eqs.tex: Ā = exp( ΔA ) ,      B̄ = (ΔA)⁻¹ ( exp(A) − I ) · ΔB          (zero-order hold discretisation)
eqs.where: Δ is the timescale parameter converting the continuous system to a discrete one

eqs.tex: hₖ = Ā hₖ₋₁ + B̄ xₖ ,   yₖ = C hₖ + D xₖ        ⟺        K̄ = ( CB̄, CĀB̄, …, CĀ^(L−1) B̄ ) ,   y = x ⊛ K̄
eqs.where: the same model in **RNN form** (sequential, O(L) memory of the whole past) and in **CNN form** (a single long convolution, parallelisable)
eqs.latex: h_{k} = \bar{A}h_{k-1} + \bar{B}x_{k}, \quad y_{k} = C h_{k} + D x_{k}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \bar{K} = \big(C\bar{B},\; C\bar{A}\bar{B},\; \ldots,\; C\bar{A}^{L-1}\bar{B}\big),\quad y = x \circledast \bar{K}

bullets: **Why the dual form is the trick.** The recurrence gives an unbounded receptive field; the convolutional form allows parallel training. Mamba keeps both.
**What Mamba adds over S4.** B, C and Δ become **input-dependent**, giving content-adaptive behaviour rather than one fixed linear system.
**Complexity** is linear in sequence length, so linear in pixel count. The full-attention baseline runs out of memory from 48×48 to 84×84; MambaIR scales like windowed attention with a global field.

notes: Nobody expects you to derive the ZOH discretisation. Do expect: 'why is an RNN suddenly fast again?' — because the CNN form makes training parallel, and the recurrence is only used at the level of the scan.

title: Adapting a sequence model to a 2-D image
lead: Mamba was built for text, which is a line. An image is a plane. The paper's contribution is the set of restoration-specific repairs needed to make the transfer work — and it names the two ways it fails without them.

bullets: **Local pixel forgetting.** To run the state-space equation, the feature map must be flattened into a sequence. Two pixels that are vertically adjacent may land hundreds of steps apart in that sequence, so the model forgets its own neighbourhood.
**Channel redundancy.** The *excessive hidden state number* produces highly redundant channels, wasting capacity.

**The fixes, inside the Residual State Space Block (RSSB):** a local convolution to restore neighbourhood awareness, and **channel attention** to suppress redundancy — plus a learnable factor controlling the skip connection.

Ablation: removing the convolution costs Urban100 accuracy (34.15 → 34.04); removing convolution *and* channel attention gives 34.06; replacing the block with an MLP gives 34.22 against the 34.15 baseline configuration.

**Four-directional scan.** The feature map is unfolded in four directions and the results summed, so no single raster order dominates. Ablation: one-direction 34.06, two-direction 33.96, four-direction (baseline) 34.15 on Urban100.

**Three stages**, structurally identical to SwinIR: shallow feature extraction (one 3×3 convolution) → deep feature extraction (stacked RSSBs grouped into RSSGs) → high-quality reconstruction aggregating shallow and deep features.
**Real noise:** SIDD 39.89 dB, DND **40.04 dB** — the best DND figure in the table, 0.01 dB above Restormer.
**Super-resolution**, where the receptive field matters most: MambaIR outperforms SwinIR by **0.41 dB on Manga109 at ×2**.

foot: **A Stage 2 finding worth knowing.** MambaIR's own repository changelog records that published complexity figures computed with `thop` were wrong and were later corrected. The model also cannot be imported at all without compiled CUDA extensions — `ModuleNotFoundError: mamba_ssm`. That is a deployment fact no paper reports, and it appears again on slide 77. `[measured]`
cite: MambaIR24 abstract, §3.2, §4.2, Tables 1, 2, 5, 6 · repository `csguoh/MambaIR`, commit 33d7b34 [measured]
notes: The import failure is a real Stage 2 result and a good one to volunteer. It shows you ran the code rather than reading about it.

title: Three live answers, and no winner
lead: The honest ending to Part V, and the reason this narrative closes on an open question rather than a conclusion. Each of these is current, each is credible, and they disagree about what the operator should be.

cards.p: Attend over channels, keep depth-wise convolution for locality. Linear in pixels. **26.1 M parameters.** Best-in-class on Gaussian grayscale, first method past 40 dB on both SIDD and DND. Slowest of the three on CPU by a wide margin. `[measured: 10.44 s at 256²]`^5^

No attention, no activation functions. Claims the gains were never attention's to begin with. **116.0 M parameters and still 5.5× faster than Restormer on CPU**, because 1×1 and depth-wise convolutions map onto optimised GEMM paths. 40.30 dB on SIDD. `[measured: 1.90 s at 256²]`^5^

Global receptive field at linear cost via a selective SSM with four-directional scanning. Best DND result at 40.04 dB. Cannot run without compiled CUDA extensions, which is a genuine deployment constraint rather than a footnote. `[measured: import fails]`^5^

The orthogonal answer, and arguably the most practical. **9.7 M parameters**, smallest of the four, with a synthetic degradation pipeline built to survive real photographs rather than benchmarks. `[measured: 1.69 s at 256²]`^5^

foot: **Say this in the defence.** A narrative that ends 'and then X won' would be false. The field currently holds three architectural answers and one data-side answer to the same bottleneck, published across three years, none of which has displaced the others. That is what an unresolved research question looks like from the inside.
cite: Restormer22 · NAFNet22 · MambaIR24 · SCUNet23 · parameter counts and CPU latencies [measured], see slide 76
notes: This is the intellectual high point of the deck. The willingness to end on an open question is what separates a literature review from a synthesis, and the brief grades synthesis.

A `.pth`, plus ~50 gradient steps per image

title: The classical prior is a while loop you can read
lead: `scikit-image 0.26.0`, `restoration/_denoise.py`, `denoise_tv_chambolle`. The structure below is the Chambolle projection algorithm as implemented there.

lines: p    = np.zeros((image.ndim,) + image.shape, dtype=...)  # dual variable
d = -p.sum(0)                 # divergence of the dual field
E += weight * norm.sum()     # ← λ·Φ(x), the prior, one line
p /= norm                    # projection onto the dual ball
if i == 0: E_init = E; E_previous = E
if np.abs(E_previous - E) < eps * E_init:  break  # ← convergence
bullets: **Four things are visible on one screen, and they characterise the entire era.** (1) `weight` *is* λ — the prior's strength is a function argument a human passes. (2) `norm.sum()` *is* Φ(x) = ‖∇x‖₁ — the prior itself, in one line of arithmetic you can read and differentiate by hand. (3) The `while` loop is the test-time optimisation. (4) The `break` on relative energy change is the stopping criterion.

**Nothing persists.** There is no state, no file, no checkpoint. Call the function on a second image and every one of these iterations runs again from scratch. That is bottleneck 1, expressed as control flow.
**The contrast to hold in mind for the next slide.** Here the prior is *readable and untrainable*. In three slides it becomes *trainable and unreadable*. That trade is the whole of the deep era.

cite: measured — `scikit-image` 0.26.0, installed from PyPI and read
notes: This is the classical exhibit precisely because it is so small. One screen of NumPy against one screen of PyTorch is a sharper argument than any prose comparison.

title: DnCNN is a list comprehension
lead: `cszn/KAIR`, `models/network_dncnn.py`. The reference PyTorch implementation, by DnCNN's own first author. Verbatim.

lines: assert 'R' in act_mode or 'L' in act_mode
for _ in range(nb-2)]        # ← the whole network
bullets: **The architecture is one line.** `m_body` is a list comprehension of `nb-2` identical blocks. The three layer types from slide 32 are literally `m_head`, `m_body`, `m_tail`. There is no architectural cleverness to read because there is none in the paper.

**`mode='C'+act_mode` is the whole layer grammar.** `'CBR'` = Convolution → BatchNorm → ReLU for the body; `'CR'` = Convolution → ReLU for the head; `'C'` = Convolution alone for the tail. Exactly the paper's Fig. 1, encoded as a three-character string.

**`return x-n` is the paper's central idea, in eight characters.** Note the subtlety: the *paper's network* outputs v̂, and the subtraction happens outside. KAIR folds the subtraction inside `forward`, so the module returns the clean image. The residual mapping is still what the weights learn — only the boundary of the module moved.

**Where is the prior?** Nowhere in this file. It is in the `.pth` checkpoint this class will load. The file describes a *shape*; the prior is the tensor poured into it. This is the moment the prior stops being readable.

cite: measured — `cszn/KAIR`, `models/network_dncnn.py`, verbatim
notes: Best single slide for the 'do you understand the code' question. Put the TV while-loop and this side by side mentally: the prior moved from line 11 of one file into a binary file that is not in the repository at all.

title: Noise2Noise is an if-statement, and P2N is three forward passes
lead: The strongest evidence that the data branch is a supervision story rather than an architecture story is that its code contains almost no architecture.

bullets: The repository is **TensorFlow** — the last major denoiser released outside PyTorch. Everything in Part V and everything after 2019 in Part IV is PyTorch. The migration is visible as a single dated boundary in the field's source history.

The change from supervised training is structurally one branch: the target tensor is either the clean image or a second noisy image. The network, the optimiser, the schedule and the loss are untouched.
**The theorem from slide 43 costs one conditional.** That asymmetry — a substantial statistical result, a trivial code change — is the whole reason the paper landed.
The network class is **`UNet_n2n_un`** and its channel widths match the 2018 Noise2Noise U-Net exactly. Seven years on, the backbone is named after its predecessor.

`noise_estimation_loss` does not merely score an output — it **constructs the inputs**: run the model on y, estimate the noise, add it back with `+` and `−`, then run the model twice more and compare the two *outputs*.
**Three forward passes per step**, and passes two and three operate on tensors that did not exist before pass one. This is why calling P2N *a new loss function* is wrong.
One function implements **all** the competing self-supervised paradigms behind a `--mode` flag. The whole data branch fits in one file.

foot: **A caveat we found in the code and would not overstate.** Two of those `--mode` branches feed RDC-constructed data to Noise2Void and Noise2Noise. The paper itself states this data is unsuitable for them, because the noise in RDC-constructed images is **correlated**, which collapses their training. Those branches are a documented negative result, not a fair comparison — and reading the flag table without reading the paper would lead you to the opposite conclusion.
cite: measured — `NVlabs/noise2noise` commit 7355519; `Li-Tong-621/P2N-plus` commit 8a117db · P2N25 on RDC data unsuitability
notes: The correlated-noise caveat is a genuine rigour point and was a correction we made during Stage 2. It shows the code and the paper being read against each other.

title: One `rearrange` is the difference between O(HW·HW) and O(C·C)
lead: `swz30/Restormer`, `basicsr/models/archs/restormer_arch.py`, `Attention.forward`. Verbatim. The claim of linear complexity is not in a comment — it is in the tensor layout.

lines: q = rearrange(q, 'b (head c) h w -> b head c (h w)', head=self.num_heads)
k = rearrange(k, 'b (head c) h w -> b head c (h w)', head=self.num_heads)
v = rearrange(v, 'b (head c) h w -> b head c (h w)', head=self.num_heads)
out = rearrange(out, 'b head c (h w) -> b (head c) h w',
bullets: **Read the einops pattern.** `'b (head c) h w -> b head c (h w)'` puts **pixels on the last axis and channels second-to-last**. In standard spatial attention it is the other way round.

**Therefore `q @ k.transpose(-2,-1)` has shape (C/head) × (C/head)**, not (HW) × (HW). At level 1 with dim = 48 and 1 head, that is a 48×48 matrix regardless of whether the image is 256×256 or 4000×3000. The paper's linear-complexity claim is exactly this line.

**`F.normalize` along the pixel axis** makes the product a cosine similarity between channels — the cross-covariance the paper describes — and `self.temperature` is a learned per-head scale replacing the fixed 1/√d_k.

**`qkv_dwconv` is the locality the paper insists on**, and the ablation on slide 55 measures its worth at 0.15 dB. Removing one `groups=dim ∗ 3` convolution costs more than most architectural papers gain.

**Why it is nonetheless slow on CPU.** Three `rearrange` calls force tensor-layout changes, and attention matmuls are poorly served by a CPU backend. Measured: **10.44 s at 256×256**, the slowest model we ran. `[measured]`

cite: measured — `swz30/Restormer`, `restormer_arch.py`, `Attention.forward`, verbatim
notes: 'Show me where the attention is actually linear' is the most likely code question in the whole defence. Be able to point at the rearrange pattern and say which axis the pixels are on.

title: SimpleGate and SCA are smaller than their descriptions
lead: `megvii-research/NAFNet`, `basicsr/models/archs/NAFNet_arch.py`. Verbatim. The paper spends two pages deriving these; the implementation is four lines and a `Sequential`.

lines: return x1 * x2                  # ← replaces GELU entirely
x = self.sg(x)                     # SimpleGate: halves the channels
y = inp + x * self.beta                 # learned residual scale
bullets: **`x.chunk(2, dim=1)` then `x1 ∗ x2`.** Compare with GELU's implementation: `0.5x(1+tanh[√(2/π)(x+0.044715x³)])`. The paper's claim that the activation is unnecessary is not rhetoric — the replacement is genuinely a channel split and a multiply.

**`self.sca` contains no nonlinearity at all.** Compare to standard channel attention, which is pool → 1×1 → ReLU → 1×1 → Sigmoid. Two activations removed, and slide 58 measures the result as **+0.03 dB**, not a loss.

**`self.beta` and `self.gamma` are learned scalars initialised to zero** — `skip-init`, which means the block starts as an identity and training decides how much of it to switch on. This is a stability device, not an architectural claim, and it does not appear in the paper's block diagram.

**Where the parameters live.** Width doubles per level, so the 12 middle blocks run at 1024 channels; each `NAFBlock` costs roughly 7c², giving 12 × 7 × 1024² ≈ **88 M of the 116 M total in the bottleneck alone**. `[measured]`

**Why it is fast despite being large.** 1×1 and depth-wise convolutions map onto highly optimised GEMM kernels. Measured: **1.90 s at 256×256 — 5.5× faster than Restormer with 4.4× the parameters.** `[measured]`

cite: measured — `megvii-research/NAFNet`, `NAFNet_arch.py`, verbatim
notes: The beta/gamma skip-init detail is a good one to have: it is in the code, mentioned only briefly in the paper, and shows you read past the block diagram.

Name a model string, options resolve it
One flag selects the training paradigm

(2) Between 2017 and 2022 the unit of reproducibility moved from *a script you edit* to *a config you version-control*, which is why modern papers can honestly claim exact reproduction.

title: Where the noise is added, and why that choice matters
lead: The brief asks how modern data pipelines work. The interesting axis is not the `Dataset` boilerplate — it is *when* the degradation is applied, because that determines what the network can possibly learn.

bullets: **Offline.** Generate noisy/clean pairs once, write them to disk, and read them during training. Deterministic and fast, but the network sees each noise realisation many times and can memorise it.

**On-the-fly, in `__getitem__`.** Draw a fresh noise realisation for every sample, every epoch. The network never sees the same corrupted patch twice, which is a powerful implicit regulariser — and it is free.
**DnCNN, 2017:** patches cropped from 400 images, noise added per sample, σ drawn from [0, 55] for the blind model. 128 × 3 000 patches of 50×50.^1^

**SCUNet, 2023:** the entire degradation chain — Gaussian, Poisson, speckle, JPEG, ISP-simulated sensor noise, resizing, with random shuffling and double degradation — is executed **per sample, at load time**. The dataloader is the contribution.^2^

right.h: What is in every modern pipeline
bullets: **Random crop** to a fixed patch size. 40–55 px in DnCNN; 128 px rising to 384 px in Restormer's^3^ progressive schedule; 256 px in NAFNet^5^; 128 px in MambaIR's^4^ denoising configuration.

**Geometric augmentation only.** Horizontal and vertical flips, and 90°/180°/270° rotations. Notably absent: colour jitter, cutout, mixup — anything that alters intensity statistics would corrupt the very quantity being estimated.
**Batch size traded against patch size.** Restormer explicitly reduces batch size as patch size grows *to maintain a similar time per optimisation step*.
**Real-noise datasets skip synthesis entirely.** SIDD ships 320 captured noisy/clean scene pairs. There is no noise model in that pipeline — the camera is the noise model.

foot: **The one line to take away.** In 2017 the data pipeline was infrastructure. By 2023 — in SCUNet, and in the whole data branch of Part IV — the data pipeline *is the method*.
cite: DnCNN17 §IV-A · SCUNet23 §3.2 · Restormer22 §4 · MambaIR24 §4.1 · NAFNet22 §5.1
notes: 'In 2017 the pipeline was infrastructure; by 2023 it is the method' is a line worth memorising. It connects Part VI back to Parts IV and V in one sentence.

title: What modern denoisers actually optimise — and what they conspicuously do not
lead: The brief asks specifically about the modern loss functions being used. The finding is a negative one and it is more interesting than the positive list.

cards.p: `L1 loss for 300K iterations`.^1^ No perceptual term, no adversarial term. The most-cited restoration Transformer of the decade optimises mean absolute error.
The negative of the evaluation metric, computed per image before the batch mean. Optimising the metric directly — honest, and a reminder that the metric is the target.^2^

An ℓ_r loss with r **decreasing during training** from 2 toward 1.5 or 0 — moving the estimator from the mean toward the median and beyond, as the model's own estimates become trustworthy. `[measured]`^3^

Essentially absent from denoising, in contrast to super-resolution, where SRGAN-style losses are standard. **Reason:** denoising is evaluated by fidelity to a known ground truth, and a GAN that hallucinates plausible texture scores worse even when it looks better. The metric constrains the loss.^4^

foot: **The honest caveat.** That last card is an inference from what we read across five repositories, not a claim any of these papers makes. It is labelled as a reading, and if a TA challenges it, the correct response is that we observed the absence rather than that a paper asserted it.
cite: Restormer22 §4 · NAFNet22 §5.1 · measured — P2N-plus loss code · reading
notes: The perceptual-loss absence is a strong observation and an obvious question hook. Do not overclaim it — say 'we observed' and name the five repositories.

title: The prior became a file you download
lead: This is the brief's sharpest comparison: how pre-trained weights are used today versus older manual feature-extraction methods. The contrast is total, and it is best stated in terms of what each era ships.

bullets: **What ships:** an algorithm, plus constants a human chose.
**Reuse:** none. Every image restarts from nothing. Nothing computed on image 1 helps image 2.
**Adaptation to a new domain:** re-derive the prior, or re-tune the constants by hand, and hope.
**Reproducibility:** depends on matching the author's parameter table, which is often in prose rather than code.
**Where the knowledge lives:** in the paper.
**What ships:** a `.pth` file — a serialised `state_dict`, a dictionary mapping layer names to tensors. Downloaded once, reused indefinitely.
**Loading:** `model.load_state_dict(torch.load(path))`, with `strict=True` by default so a shape mismatch fails loudly rather than silently.
**Distribution:** GitHub Releases, Google Drive links, and increasingly Hugging Face model cards that carry the architecture, the training data, the metrics and the licence as structured metadata.
**Adaptation:** fine-tune, or use the weights as an initialisation — which is precisely what P2N does before its per-image optimisation.
**Where the knowledge lives:** in the tensors. The repository describes only a shape.

foot: **The consequence that is easy to miss.** Because the weights are a file and the architecture is a string in a YAML, a modern denoiser is *two decoupled artefacts*. You can ship a better checkpoint without touching the code, and swap the architecture without retraining the pipeline. The classical era had no such separation, and that is a large part of why it could not compound.
cite: measured — checkpoint loading in KAIR, Restormer, NAFNet, SCUNet · brief §2 on pre-trained weights
notes: This is the slide that directly answers a question the brief asks in so many words. Expect it to be asked and answer with the two-artefact framing.
citeN: measured — checkpoint loading in KAIR, Restormer, NAFNet, SCUNet

kicker: A deployment detail no paper reports
title: Every model pads — and they all pad differently
lead: A U-Net that downsamples k times requires input dimensions divisible by 2ᵏ. Every architecture-branch model solves this with the same pad-then-crop idiom and a different constant, which becomes a real problem the moment two are chained in one pipeline.
foot: **A factor of eight separates the extremes, and the padding mode differs too** — zero padding injects a hard artificial edge, reflection and replication do not. Feed a 1000×1000 image to SCUNet and 26 rows and columns of replicated content are silently invented, processed, and cropped away. None of this appears in any of the four papers. It is exactly the class of fact the brief means by *practical deployment realities*, and it is only visible by reading `forward`.
cite: measured — verbatim from the four repositories at the commits on slide 65
notes: A favourite because it is concrete, verifiable, and invisible from the literature. Good answer to 'what did you learn from the code that you could not learn from the papers?'

title: Seven architectures, instantiated and timed
lead: Each model was instantiated from its own repository at the commit on slide 65, in the configuration that repository uses for denoising. Parameters are `sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())`. Latency is the mean of three forward passes at 256×256 after one warm-up, under `torch.no_grad()`, **CPU only**, PyTorch 2.13.0, no CUDA.
foot: **Two caveats, stated before they are asked.** (1) Absolute CPU latencies are **not** comparable to published GPU timings — the *ratios* are the informative quantity. (2) The forward passes used **random tensors**, so no PSNR or SSIM was measured here; every quality number in this deck comes from the papers, and every timing and parameter count on this slide comes from us. The two are never mixed in one column.
cite: measured — Stage 2 benchmark, CPU-only container, PyTorch 2.13.0
notes: Declaring the random-tensor caveat unprompted is important. The obvious attack is 'did you verify the PSNRs yourself?' — the answer is no, and saying so first is much stronger than conceding it.

title: Four conclusions, none of them visible from a paper
lead: These are the readings that justify having run the code at all. Each contradicts something a reader would reasonably assume from the published tables.

cards.p: NAFNet carries **4.4× Restormer's parameters and runs 5.5× faster** on identical hardware. NAFNet is 1×1 and depth-wise convolutions on fast GEMM paths; Restormer's `rearrange` calls force layout changes and its attention matmuls are poorly served by a CPU backend. **'More efficient' is meaningless without naming the metric — parameters, MACs, or wall-clock — and the device.**^1^

Switching Symmetric Prior Injection on **reduces** P2N+'s parameters by 6.7% (0.991 M → 0.925 M), because `Symlayer` routes through a half-width bottleneck — yet latency rises **2.5×** (0.286 s → 0.710 s), because every layer is evaluated twice, on x and on −x.^1^ This is the exact opposite of what a parameter table predicts, and it is invisible unless you run it.

cards.h: The oldest model is the smallest and still not the fastest
cards.p: DnCNN is the smallest model in the table at 0.668 M and is nonetheless **slower than the 0.991 M P2N+ backbone**, because DnCNN is 20 sequential full-resolution 3×3 convolutions at 64 channels while a U-Net does most of its work at reduced resolution.^1^ Depth at full resolution is expensive in a way parameter count does not show.

cards.h: Some models simply do not run
cards.p: MambaIR raises `ModuleNotFoundError: mamba_ssm` without compiled CUDA extensions.^1^ That is not a gap in our experiment — it *is* the result. A model that cannot be imported on a CPU machine has a deployment profile fundamentally different from one that can, and no paper reports this. The repository's own changelog^2^ also records that published complexity figures computed with `thop` were wrong.

cite: measured — Stage 2 benchmark · MambaIR repository changelog
notes: Reading (a) is the one to lead with. It is a clean, falsifiable, counterintuitive claim backed by a number you produced, which is exactly what the brief's Practical Integration criterion rewards.

title: Comparative Analysis
lead: Eighteen years of numbers, assembled under rules strict enough that the comparison means something.

items: Real noise — where the assumption breaks
The whole arc in one view

cite: brief §6
notes: Open with the rules slide, not with a table. Numbers assembled without a stated methodology are the easiest thing in a deck to attack.

title: Five rules, so that the comparison survives scrutiny
lead: Cross-paper PSNR tables are the most commonly abused artefact in this field. These are the constraints we imposed on ourselves, and they are worth stating before any number appears.

bullets: **1 · No number was computed by us.** Every PSNR and SSIM in Part VII is reproduced from a published table, with the paper and table named. We ran no denoising evaluation of our own, because doing it correctly would require matching each paper's crop, border, colour-space and rounding conventions — and a table that mixes our numbers with theirs would be worse than useless.

**2 · Rows come from one table wherever possible.** When comparing DnCNN to Restormer, both figures are taken from Restormer's Table 4, where the authors evaluated both under one protocol. Taking DnCNN's number from its own paper and Restormer's from its own would silently compare two different evaluation scripts.

**3 · Timings and quality are never mixed in one column.** Every quality number is from a paper; every latency and parameter count is from our own measurements on stated hardware. The two are reported in separate tables and labelled.

title: Real noise, and the perception–distortion trade-off
lead: The two open problems for which this deck already contains hard evidence, rather than speculation.

cards.p: SCUNet's^1^ abstract states the position as of 2023: *a general-purpose blind denoising method for real images remains unsolved.* The evidence on slide 82 is stark — DnCNN scores 23.66 dB on SIDD. SCUNet's answer is to synthesise realistic degradations; Restormer and NAFNet's answer is to train directly on SIDD's 320 captured scenes.^3^ **Neither generalises to an unseen camera with an unseen ISP**, and no benchmark currently measures that.

cards.h: Noise is a pipeline, not a distribution
cards.p: Real noise is read noise plus shot noise in the raw domain, then transformed by demosaicing, white balance, colour conversion, tone mapping and gamma — each of which correlates it spatially and across channels. SCUNet^1^ models this by *inverting* the ISP, adding noise in raw, and running it forward again. That is an engineering simulation of a physical device, not a probability model, and it is as good as the device model it assumes.

Every loss in Part VI is L1, L2 or PSNR. All three recover a conditional mean, and the conditional mean of the plausible clean images is smoother than any of them. **Noise2Noise^2^ names this mechanism explicitly:** an L2-trained regressor *learns to output the average of all plausible explanations, which results in spatial blurriness*. The field's default objective is structurally biased toward the very over-smoothing that BM3D was criticised for.

Perceptual and adversarial losses would fix the blur and would score *worse* on PSNR, because they hallucinate plausible texture that does not match the ground truth pixel for pixel. As long as leaderboards are PSNR-ranked, the incentive points the wrong way. This is why, as slide 73 observes, perceptual losses are common in super-resolution and essentially absent from denoising.^4^

notes: The observation that Noise2Noise names the blur mechanism while proposing an L2 method is a nice piece of close reading. It is in §2 of the paper, in the super-resolution example.

title: Efficiency, evaluation, and the self-supervision gap
lead: Three further open problems, each of which this deck has produced direct evidence for rather than inherited from a survey.

cards.p: Slide 76 produced three incompatible rankings of the same models from parameters, wall-clock and quality — and Restormer's^4^ FLOP claim is a fourth. MambaIR's own changelog concedes its published `thop` complexity figures were wrong. **The field has no agreed cost metric**, which makes efficiency claims across papers close to meaningless and is why our benchmark reports the counting method alongside every number.^1^

BSD68 σ=25 moved 0.36 dB in the five years from DnCNN to Restormer^4^, while Urban100 moved five times as much and SIDD moved sixteen decibels. A benchmark that cannot distinguish 2017 from 2022 is no longer measuring the thing the field is working on. **New capability is arriving faster than the instruments to detect it.**

N2V^2^ trails supervised training by 1.35 dB on BSD68 and sits below BM3D. P2N's^3^ contribution is removing the *information loss*, not closing the quality gap, and it still pays per-image test-time optimisation. **Bottleneck 2 is mitigated, not closed** — and the domains that need it most, microscopy and medical imaging, are precisely those where no clean reference exists to measure the remaining gap.

cards.h: The two branches have never merged
cards.p: This is our own observation and the structural claim of the deck. P2N^3^ ships the 2018 Noise2Noise U-Net verbatim; Restormer, NAFNet and MambaIR^4^ all assume paired data. **Nobody has published a state-space or Transformer backbone trained by RDC/DCS supervision.** Whether the branches compose or conflict is, as far as we found, an open and apparently untested question.

title: The thesis, restated

body.q:
Image denoising is the cleanest available case study in how computer vision replaced hand-designed priors with learned ones.

Its history divides into four eras separated by three identifiable bottlenecks — manual prior design, the clean-data requirement, and the receptive-field limits of convolution. Each bottleneck was named by the paper that broke it, so the arc is evidenced from the primary sources rather than imposed in hindsight.

In 2018 the response forked. One branch changed what the network is shown; the other changed what the network is. They have never merged.

And because the field currently holds three competing answers to the third bottleneck and none to the first open problem, the story ends in a genuine open question rather than a winner.

lead: A gap that is stated is a smaller problem than a gap that is found. These are every known weakness in this deck.

**The DnCNN runtime table mixes devices.** Classical methods are timed on CPU, learned methods on GPU, and the paper states that GPU times for CSF and TNRD were copied from their original papers. We reproduce this caveat wherever we reproduce the numbers.
